---
name: xsk-execute-plan
description: Execute a small plan or request as context-isolated subagent tasks sharing one writable workspace, tracked in a .xsk/runs/ ledger, with one confirmation gate, no per-task code review, and unified acceptance. Explicit invocation only.
---

# xsk-execute-plan

Execute a small, decision-light plan or request through context-isolated subagent tasks that share the same writable workspace, so the main conversation keeps only compact results instead of file contents. A persistent run ledger under `.xsk/runs/` records every task and its acceptance state, so a mid-run context compression loses nothing that matters.

It fits tasks that are simple to decide but heavy to execute: the work reads and writes far more content than the task description itself (several files, several steps). It is the wrong tool for trivia: a one-file tweak or a single command is cheaper done inline, and dispatching a subagent for it costs more than it saves.

## When to use

This skill is explicitly invoked only: `/xsk-execute-plan`, a direct request such as "use xsk-execute-plan to run this", or the user's selection of the `xsk-execute-plan` next action offered by `xsk-think`. As a deliberate local rule that overrides the shared intent-matching convention below, it never self-triggers on execution intent, so it cannot collide with a harness's own plan or execution modes.

Selection from `xsk-think` is an explicit invocation of this skill, but invocation starts intake only. It never means immediate task dispatch and never bypasses this skill's task-breakdown and acceptance confirmation gate.

It accepts two kinds of input:

- a concrete execution plan, such as an approved `xsk-think` design
- a small plain-language request that needs no real design work first

## How it works

**1. Intake, ground lightly, and confirm dispatch capability.** Restate the goal in one sentence. A concrete plan (such as an approved `xsk-think` design) is taken as given; a small plain-language request gets a quick scan of the directly relevant code and config, not a full design pass. Derive the run slug from the goal line using the pattern `^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$`.

Before offering any recovery choice and before opening a run ledger, verify that the current harness can dispatch at least one subagent that can write to the same workspace and return a compact result. If writable-workspace subagent dispatch is unavailable, stop before offering a recovery choice or writing a ledger. Recommend direct execution, or return to `xsk-think` to reduce, split, or revise the plan. Never silently degrade `xsk-execute-plan` into inline execution. This is a one-time capability check, not a precondition re-tested before each ledger line.

**2. Establish a committed Git baseline, resolve prior state, then preflight the hard rules.** Run `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` and `git rev-parse --verify HEAD` before offering a recovery choice or writing a ledger. If the workspace is not a Git worktree or has no valid `HEAD` commit, stop without writing anything and explain that `xsk-execute-plan` requires a committed Git baseline. A non-Git directory and an unborn repository are unsupported; never invent an empty base commit or claim that an unavailable actual diff was verified. For a new run or confirmed restart, record the full current `HEAD` object ID as the base commit. For resume or reuse, read the base commit from the existing ledger, verify that the object still exists, and never replace it with current `HEAD`. If current `HEAD` differs from that recorded base, reuse is disabled. A resume may continue only when the recorded base is still an ancestor of current `HEAD` and the user confirms the movement; otherwise report it as interruption ambiguity before any further dispatch and require explicit resolution or a restart against current `HEAD`.

The base commit is an active invariant, not only an intake value. Re-run `git rev-parse --verify HEAD` immediately before every task dispatch, after every subagent returns before attributing its writes, before unified acceptance, and immediately before writing the final fingerprint. Equal to the recorded base, carry on. Different but with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <recorded base> HEAD` succeeding, history only moved forward: a plan may legitimately include a commit and the user may commit alongside the run, so report the movement, ask once whether it was expected, and on confirmation record the new object ID as the current base while keeping the original and the reason in the ledger. Only when the recorded base is no longer an ancestor was history rewritten under the run: do not dispatch, attribute output, verify, or mint a fingerprint against it, preserve the worktree, record any returned task as `failed` with repository-movement ambiguity and the observable terminal path states, and require explicit resolution or restart.

If `.xsk/runs/<slug>.md` already exists:

- With `status: running` or `status: failed`, first compute the current invocation's input identity from its supplied `source`, exact goal, and complete plan or request text using the scheme in step 3, and compare it with the recorded one before offering resume. Only an exact match may offer the user resume or restart. If it differs, is missing, uses an unrecognized scheme, or cannot be reproduced from the complete current input, resume is unavailable: present the old task state as history, offer only restart, and require the replacement execution envelope to be rebuilt and explicitly confirmed through steps 3 and 4 before any old task can be dispatched. On a matching resume, continue from the current worktree, never by rolling source files back: keep done tasks, and re-dispatch only the unfinished tasks whose state is pending or failed. A task left at `in-flight` was dispatched and never reported back, so its writes may be fully, partly, or not at all applied: never re-dispatch it blind. Inspect its allowed paths, report what is already there, and ask the user whether to re-dispatch it as the next attempt, accept the existing state and mark it done, or fail it. Accepting existing state as `done` must first perform the same independent touched-path derivation, terminal output fingerprint capture, and dirty-overlap preservation check as a normally returned task. If all tasks are already done, resume at unified acceptance and reporting instead of dispatching them again.
- Restart also uses the current worktree as its baseline. It may overwrite the ledger after confirmation, but it never resets, reverts, or otherwise rolls back existing source changes.
- With `status: done`, compare exactly two identities, both recomputed from material that still exists: the current invocation's input identity against the recorded one, and a freshly computed workspace fingerprint against the one recorded in `## Result`, matching the exact path set as well as every path-state fingerprint. Do not ask the run to re-derive the old execution envelope and match it: a fresh decomposition of the same plan will not reproduce the recorded task definitions verbatim, so that comparison could never pass and would only dress a blanket refusal as a check.

  When the input identity differs, is missing, or cannot be reproduced from the complete current input, present the old result as history only and offer only a new run with a newly confirmed envelope: the old task outputs do not prove that a revised plan was implemented. When the input identity matches but the workspace fingerprint differs or is missing, reuse stays off the table, but fresh unified acceptance against the current state may be offered alongside a new run, provided all historical baseline and terminal checkpoint evidence is intact; apply the resume ambiguity rules before verification. Only when both identities match may reuse without dispatch be offered alongside a new run. A result that fails any required comparison must never be reported as verified. A `done` run whose result was already reported and consumed may instead be retired by deleting its ledger and any companion baseline artifacts: they are transient state whose stale claims only mislead once the worktree has moved on.

A resume reuses the execution envelope recorded in the ledger, including its pre-existing dirty-path baseline: the worktree now also holds this run's own writes, so recapturing that baseline would misread them as the user's work. Before dispatching anything, compare current path-state fingerprints with the recorded dirty baselines and terminal task-output fingerprints. A dirty path whose fingerprint still matches is untouched user work. Matching the most recent terminal `done` or `failed` fingerprint proves only that the task-end state is unchanged; path membership or a compact result alone is never proof of run ownership, and a match never transfers ownership of pre-run dirty content. A dirty-overlap path remains subject to its separately recorded user-change preservation proof. Anything with no matching baseline, or whose latest task-output fingerprint no longer matches, is a user change or ambiguity that appeared during the interruption. Report it and treat it as the user's, never as this run's to overwrite. A resume does not re-run the confirmation gate. If ordinary envelope fields do not cover every unfinished task but all historical baseline and checkpoint evidence is intact, extend the envelope and re-confirm it through steps 3 and 4 before dispatching anything. A missing or invalid base, dirty-overlap baseline, companion artifact, input identity, or required terminal output checkpoint cannot be reconstructed from the current worktree during resume. The same is true of a missing ignored-state baseline, coverage record, or acceptance-command checkpoint needed to attribute post-command writes. Report the affected paths as ambiguous and require explicit resolution or restart; never recapture current state and call it the original baseline. A restart always rebuilds and re-confirms the envelope, and replaces any old companion baseline artifacts only after the restart choice.

The resume, restart, or reuse choice is exceptional recovery, not the normal confirmation gate. A prior `failed` run is never overwritten silently.

Scan `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and any repo rules or config for constraints that would forbid or force a choice. Keep this brief: it is a check, not a study.

**3. Decompose and define the execution envelope.** Produce an ordered task list with at least one entry and record each task's dependencies and execution order. Define the acceptance criteria before anything executes. For every task, name its expected write paths, the tolerated side-effect paths that correct work legitimately touches (regenerated output, lockfiles, formatter fallout), and the project verification commands that cover it. For every verification command, also name its own expected and tolerated write footprint, including snapshots, generated files, and formatter output, or write `none` when it is expected to be read-only.

Record the input identity as `xsk-execute-plan-input-v1:sha256:<64 lowercase hexadecimal characters>`. Build the preimage by writing the literal `source` value, the exact goal line, and the complete plan or request text exactly as supplied, in that order, each followed by one newline, into a temporary file, then hash that file with the platform's SHA-256 utility (`shasum -a 256` or `sha256sum`). The digest must come from running that tool. A hash written from inspection is a fabricated identity, and a fabricated identity is worse than none, because every later resume and reuse decision rests on it. When no SHA-256 utility is available, record `xsk-execute-plan-input-v1:text` instead and store the source, goal, and complete input text verbatim in the ledger; a later comparison then compares that text directly. A missing or unrecognized scheme is an identity failure, never permission to guess another serialization.

Capture the pre-existing dirty paths before dispatch. Also establish an ignored-state baseline, and scope it deliberately: cover every ignored path that falls inside a declared task or verification-command footprint, plus any additional ignored root the user names at the gate. A workspace-wide walk is not required and is rarely affordable, since one dependency or build directory routinely holds far more files than the whole run touches, and demanding it would make the skill unusable in exactly the repositories it targets. Within that scope, use the repository's Git ignore rules plus a filesystem walk that does not follow symlinks, consolidate nested entries into a minimal set of roots, and record deterministic recursive entry manifests that are sufficient to identify changed descendants. Record `Ignored-path coverage: complete` when every in-scope root is represented and a later scan can enumerate paths newly created under them. If an in-scope root cannot be enumerated or fingerprinted, record `Ignored-path coverage: incomplete` with the paths and reason; never silently treat the missing state as unchanged.

Treat every pre-existing ignored path, including one outside all task footprints, as user state because Git cannot supply its baseline. For every dirty path and ignored baseline root, record a path-state fingerprint that binds the index and worktree separately: exact Git index entries for every stage, including stage number, mode, and blob object ID or an absent tombstone; Git worktree status; and worktree existence, node type, mode, and content identity. Hash regular-file bytes, record a symlink target without following it, use a deterministic recursive entry manifest for a directory, and explicitly record an absent or deleted worktree tombstone. A status label such as `MM` is never a substitute for the exact index entries, because index content can change while that label and the worktree bytes stay the same. These paths belong to the user, not to this run. A bare path list cannot show later whether those changes survived, so record one fingerprint per path or consolidated ignored root.

If an expected or tolerated write path overlaps dirty or pre-existing ignored user state, a whole-file hash alone is not sufficient: after legitimate task edits, a different hash cannot prove whether the user's original change survived. Overlap includes exact equality and ancestor or descendant containment after path normalization, without following symlinks. For every overlap, prepare a comparable preservation baseline before dispatch. Preserve the index and worktree layers separately with binary-capable base-to-index and index-to-worktree patches, or with the full staged blobs, exact index entries, and full worktree content and path state. Plan to store it and any large ignored-state manifests inline in the ledger, or in an immutable `.xsk/runs/<slug>.baseline/` companion referenced by relative path and hash from the ledger when inline Markdown is unsuitable. Do not write either run artifact before the normal gate; immediately after approval, persist and hash-check all baseline evidence before any task becomes `in-flight`. Call out the ignored-path coverage and each overlap with its preservation-baseline reference explicitly in the confirmation envelope.

Mark every task that has a UI surface and record for it the reference (a design link or image), the target platform (Android, web, or desktop), and how to render and screenshot it. Also list any external, destructive, irreversible, remote, dependency-introducing, or platform-permission action that the plan may require. Write `none` when a category has no such action.

**4. One normal confirmation gate.** Show the user the complete execution envelope: the base commit, ordered tasks and dependency order, acceptance criteria, expected write paths, tolerated side-effect paths, verification commands, pre-existing dirty paths, ignored-path coverage, path-state fingerprints and overlap preservation-baseline references, UI advisory, and flagged exceptional actions. Get one explicit go-ahead. This is the only checkpoint on the normal path; a recovery choice in step 2 is exceptional. Even an approved `xsk-think` plan passes through this gate. Selecting `xsk-execute-plan` from `xsk-think` explicitly invokes this skill, but it does not approve this envelope or authorize immediate dispatch.

The workflow gate authorizes only the confirmed, local, reversible workspace changes. It never authorizes a new product decision, scope expansion, dependency introduction, external or remote mutation, destructive or irreversible action, or a platform permission prompt. If any of those is planned or appears during execution, stop before it and obtain focused user authorization. Before dispatch, record each granted exception in the execution envelope with its exact action, target, assigned task, scope, limits, and permitted attempts. The exception authorizes only those recorded terms; it does not carry to another task, retry, verifier, or fix task unless the recorded terms explicitly include it. A newly discovered decision that changes implementation also returns to the user. These exceptional authorizations do not weaken the single normal workflow gate.

**5. Open the ledger, then dispatch context-isolated tasks.** Only after the normal gate passes, write the run ledger `.xsk/runs/<slug>.md` with `status: running`:

```markdown
---
status: running | done | failed
slug: <slug>
created_at: <ISO date>
source: plan | request
---

# <goal in one line>

## Execution Envelope
- Base commit: <full Git object ID at run start; append each confirmed forward move with its reason>
- Input identity: <xsk-execute-plan-input-v1:sha256:64-lowercase-hex from a SHA-256 utility, or xsk-execute-plan-input-v1:text with the verbatim source, goal, and input recorded below>
- Dependency order: <task order>
- Expected write paths: <paths by task and verification command>
- Tolerated side-effect paths: <paths by task and verification command, or none>
- Verification commands: <commands>
- Pre-existing dirty paths: <path-state fingerprint per path; overlap preservation-baseline reference and hash, or none>
- Ignored-path coverage: <complete with baseline roots and hashes, or incomplete with paths and reason>
- UI advisory: <task details or none>
- Exceptional actions and authorizations: <action, target, assigned task, scope, limits, permitted attempts, and pending or granted status, or none>

## Acceptance
- [ ] <criterion>

## Tasks
1. [pending|in-flight|done|failed] (attempt <n>) <full task description, self-contained enough to re-dispatch, with dependencies, allowed write paths, and acceptance items> - <attempt-start footprint fingerprints and changed-path inventory; compact result; actual touched paths; terminal output path-state fingerprints; dirty-overlap preservation result>

## Result
(after all tasks: per-criterion pass/fail/skipped, verifier result, failures, actual touched paths, leftovers)
Acceptance fingerprint: <current confirmed base commit; ignored-path coverage state; exact sorted path set from Git-different, expected, tolerated, and actual-touched paths; each path's path-state fingerprint at acceptance time>
```

`source: plan` means the input was a concrete plan; `source: request` means a small plain-language request, not a `.xsk/requirements/` document. The complete plan or request is part of the input identity even when it is not repeated verbatim in the ledger. Every `## Tasks` entry carries the full task description as confirmed at the gate; a one-line stub would make resuming meaningless once the session context is gone. Immediately before persisting the approved ledger and baseline artifacts, revalidate every pre-run path-state fingerprint; if one changed while confirmation was pending, update the envelope and obtain a replacement confirmation before dispatch. Ensure `.xsk/.gitignore` contains the line `runs/` (create `.xsk/` and `.xsk/.gitignore` if absent; append the line only if it is missing; never overwrite an existing `.xsk/.gitignore`). The ledger and any `.xsk/runs/<slug>.baseline/` companion are transient execution state, not deliverables: never offer to commit them. Overwrite or remove existing run state only through the recovery choice in step 2, including the retirement of a reported `done` run offered there.

Subagents are isolated from the main conversation's context, not from one another's filesystem. They share the same writable workspace. Each task goes to one subagent with a self-contained prompt containing the applicable hard rules, the full task and acceptance items, its allowed and expected write paths, required dependency results, and a default prohibition on dependency introduction, remote or external actions, destructive or irreversible actions, and platform permission prompts. When a task has a granted exception recorded in the envelope, copy its exact action, target, scope, limits, and permitted attempts into that task's prompt as the sole exception. Keep the prohibition for everything else, and require the subagent to stop and return without acting if it would exceed the recorded exception. If the exact exception cannot be passed to the assigned task, do not dispatch it. Require the subagent to return a compact result, verification evidence, and its actual touched paths.

Order tasks by dependency. A task's write footprint is its expected write paths together with its tolerated side-effect paths: a shared lockfile or regenerated index counts even when the two tasks own different source files. Run tasks in parallel only when their footprints do not overlap and neither footprint creates ambiguity with a pre-existing dirty path; tasks with authorized external or remote actions also run serially unless their recorded targets and limits prove that they cannot conflict. When in doubt, run them serially, since parallel subagents share the same files. Before every dispatch, compare the complete footprint with its latest trusted pre-run baseline or terminal task checkpoint. Also compare the in-scope ignored roots and their manifests with the latest trusted ignored-state checkpoint. Any mismatch since that checkpoint is new user work or ambiguity: pause, protect it from the next task, and require focused resolution and an updated confirmation when the envelope changes. Never fold it silently into the old preservation proof.

The ledger is write-ahead: in the same write that sets a task's line to `in-flight` with its attempt number, record path-state fingerprints for its complete footprint, the current Git changed-path inventory, and the current ignored-state checkpoint, then dispatch it. These attempt-start records let the main workflow independently derive and validate Git-visible, ignored, and in-footprint changes while reconciling the subagent's report. After the subagent returns, rescan the in-scope ignored roots and compare every root manifest with the attempt-start checkpoint. A changed existing ignored descendant or a newly created ignored path under those roots is an independently detected touched path and enters the scope-drift flow even when the subagent omitted it. If coverage is incomplete, record the ambiguity and the affected paths, mark the acceptance criteria that depended on them `skipped` with that reason, and report it prominently. Incomplete coverage never passes as verified and is carried into the acceptance fingerprint, where a later comparison treats it as non-matching; it does not by itself fail a run whose own criteria are otherwise met. Update the task to `done` or `failed` with its terminal evidence as soon as the subagent returns. Recording state only after a task finishes would let an interruption between dispatch and result leave finished work looking like work that never started. Between tasks there is no code review and no acceptance run. The main conversation records each task's compact result, path checkpoints, and preservation evidence, all of it produced by tools rather than by reading file contents, and it judges nothing about the implementation until unified acceptance.

When the subagent returns, independently derive every detectable actual touched path from the base, attempt-start records, current Git state, ignored-state comparison, and the subagent report, including paths that are now absent; reconcile these sources rather than trusting the report alone. Capture a terminal output path-state fingerprint for every one and update the trusted ignored-state checkpoint after reconciling any ignored changes. Update a task to `done` or `failed` only in the same ledger write that records its compact result, actual touched paths, and output fingerprints. A failed task can leave partial output, so `failed` requires the same evidence as `done`. If a path or complete touched set cannot be fingerprinted, record the ambiguity and pause before dispatching dependents; never turn a path name into provenance by assumption. For a path touched by multiple terminal tasks, retain every checkpoint and use the most recent terminal fingerprint as the comparison point on resume.

For every touched dirty-overlap path, compare the base-commit state, saved pre-run index and worktree patches or full snapshots, and post-task index and worktree states after the task returns. Record concrete preservation evidence showing that the pre-existing staged and unstaged user changes survived. A changed whole-file hash or an unchanged two-letter Git status is not that evidence. If the comparison shows loss, or cannot prove preservation, mark the task `failed` for preservation ambiguity in the same terminal ledger write, keep the worktree intact, pause before dispatching dependents, and ask the user how to resolve it; do not mark the task `done` or claim that the user change was preserved. If the task failed for another reason, still record the output fingerprint and failed preservation result before stopping its dependents. Never silently restore one version over another.

Compare every task's actual touched paths with its confirmed allowed paths. Never revert an unexpected path automatically. A path the confirmed envelope already lists as a tolerated side effect is recorded in the ledger and the run carries on. Any other unexpected path is scope drift: pause before dispatching that task's dependents, keep the worktree intact, report the path and what the task wrote there, and ask the user once whether to accept it into scope or fail the task. Accepting records the path in the envelope and continues; failing marks the task failed and stops its dependents. That question is an exception check against the confirmed envelope, not the per-task code review this skill omits. When a task otherwise fails, stop its dependents, keep what finished, and report honestly. No pretended atomicity, no unbounded auto-fixing.

Any accepted scope drift or separately authorized action changes the final execution envelope, and its exact authorization terms belong in it. Any functional or UI fix attempt adds a full task definition and dependency to the final ordered task list. Persist those changes before further dispatch and again before final acceptance, so `## Result` describes the effective tasks, acceptance criteria, and envelope that actually produced the result rather than the ones first confirmed.

**6. Accept once, after all tasks.** Two tiers with different weight.

- Functional acceptance is a real signal. First run the project's own verification commands (tests, lint, build) and read the output. Immediately before each command, persist an acceptance-command checkpoint in the ledger containing the command, current Git changed-path inventory, full path-state fingerprints for its declared write footprint, and the ignored-state checkpoint. After each command returns, derive and fingerprint every detectable write, including ignored, generated, snapshot, formatter, staged, deleted, and type-changed output. In the same next ledger write, record the command's exit result and compact output evidence, actual touched paths, terminal fingerprints, and overlap result. Reconcile those writes through the same allowed-path, scope-drift, dirty-overlap preservation, and ignored-coverage rules as a task before continuing. A command failure does not excuse this reconciliation. Only after the project commands and all of their writes have been reconciled, dispatch a fresh verifier that did not implement any task. Give it the confirmed goal, acceptance criteria, execution envelope, current confirmed base commit, pre-existing dirty-path fingerprints, in-scope ignored-state baseline and post-command scan, saved index and worktree overlap patches or full snapshots, recorded overlap-preservation evidence, terminal task-output and acceptance-command fingerprints, actual touched paths, command output evidence, and the post-command actual diff derived against the recorded base commit and pre-run index and worktree states. The diff and path list must cover staged, unstaged, ignored-but-touched, untracked, deleted, and type-changed paths; construct an explicit before/after representation for paths ordinary Git diff omits. Exclude only Git metadata and this run's ledger and companion baseline artifacts from that diff; include `.xsk/.gitignore` when this run changed it. The verifier checks the implementation against the goal and criteria, independently proves that every dirty-overlap staged and unstaged user change survived, verifies scope and leftovers, and returns evidence without modifying files. Missing or inconclusive overlap evidence is a functional failure, not a pass inferred from hashes or status labels. Incomplete ignored-path coverage is not a failure by itself: it marks the criteria that depended on it `skipped`, is recorded in the fingerprint, and can never be reported as a pass. A verifier mismatch or command failure is also reported as a functional failure. Permit at most one bounded fix attempt for unified functional acceptance, then rerun the project commands, reconcile their writes, and repeat the fresh-verifier check once in that order; never loop. Dispatch that fix as its own write-ahead ledger task under the full step 5 contract: allowed paths, the drift comparison, overlap preservation, terminal output fingerprints, and the same scoped-authority contract, copying only an exact granted exception assigned to that fix task and prohibiting everything else. When the project has no runnable verification commands at all, record the command-backed acceptance criteria as `skipped` and state "functional acceptance not run" prominently in the report: `skipped` is non-failing but must never look like `pass`, the fresh verifier does not turn skipped command checks into passes, and a run with zero runnable gates must never look verified.
- UI fidelity acceptance is warning-level, never a gate. Run it only for tasks marked with a UI surface, and only when the environment can render the UI and capture a screenshot; otherwise record the affected acceptance criteria as `skipped` and use the single line "UI acceptance skipped: cannot render or screenshot here", which is not a failure, blocks nothing, and asks nothing of the user. When it runs: render, screenshot, compare against the design reference, and list concrete deviations (spacing, color, alignment, missing elements, overflow), delegating rendering, screenshots, and visual comparison to existing tools rather than building any. Dispatch a fix subagent scoped to exactly those deviations, re-render, and re-compare, at most 2 rounds by default (the user may set another bound at invocation). Every UI fix round is dispatched as its own write-ahead ledger task under the full step 5 contract too: allowed paths, the drift comparison, and the same scoped-authority contract, copying only an exact granted exception assigned to that UI fix task and prohibiting everything else. Any deviation that survives the last round goes into the report as a warning for the user to weigh; it never fails the run and never gates anything. After the last UI fix round that changed files, rerun the project's relevant functional verification commands (tests, lint, build), reconcile their writes, and only then dispatch a fresh verifier against the updated post-command diff before deriving final status; discard any earlier functional result. A revalidation failure is a functional acceptance failure and sets the ledger to `status: failed`.

After any UI fix that changed files, the functional revalidation follows the same project-commands, write-reconciliation, then fresh-verifier order. The final `done` or `failed` comes from the latest functional acceptance and task outcomes alone; fresh-verifier failure is part of functional acceptance, while UI residuals and `skipped` criteria never fail the run by themselves.

**7. Report and stop.** Fill `## Result`: each task's compact outcome, actual touched paths, and terminal output fingerprints; each acceptance command's exit result, compact output evidence, induced writes, and terminal fingerprints; the fresh verifier's conclusion; each acceptance criterion's `pass`, `fail`, or `skipped` status (with the reason when skipped); overlap-preservation evidence; ignored-path coverage; UI warnings if any; and whether functional acceptance ran. Include scope drift with how it was resolved, blocked dependents, and separately authorized actions when present. Record the acceptance fingerprint as a workspace fingerprint: the current confirmed base commit, the ignored-path coverage state, plus the exact sorted union of every path whose index or worktree state differs from that commit and every expected, tolerated, or actual touched path, including ignored output, empty directories, untracked, deleted, mode-changed, and type-changed paths, with each path's full path-state fingerprint. Exclude Git metadata and this run's ledger and companion baseline artifacts to avoid a self-referential fingerprint, but include `.xsk/.gitignore` when changed. A later comparison must match the exact path set as well as every entry; an added or missing path is a mismatch. Reuse later requires this fingerprint and the input identity to match, and a fingerprint carrying incomplete coverage never matches. Produce an acceptance fingerprint only when the latest functional acceptance passed, all scope-verification evidence is conclusive, and the final status is `done`. Otherwise write `Acceptance fingerprint: not produced`, set `status: failed` for any functional or scope-verification failure, and never describe the run as verified; terminal task checkpoints are still required. Do not commit, push, or publish unless the user asks for it. Stop.

## Output

A per-task list of compact results, actual touched paths, and terminal output fingerprints; each verification command's exit result and the writes it induced; the fresh verifier's conclusion; the acceptance report with each criterion's `pass`, `fail`, or `skipped` status (including a reason for `skipped`), overlap-preservation evidence, ignored-path coverage, scope drift and UI warnings if any, and whether functional acceptance ran; and the ledger path `.xsk/runs/<slug>.md` with its final `status` (`done` or `failed`) and either its acceptance fingerprint or `Acceptance fingerprint: not produced`.

<SHARED_MASKED>
